items.title: Size matters: South Korea spared iPad mini image's potentially offensive gesture
items.content_html:
Apple has chosen to use a different image in South Korea to promote the iPad mini in South Korea, likely over fears that the version used the rest of the world might resemble an offensive gesture mocking the size of someone's manhood.

The launch of the updated iPad mini with OLED has unexpectedly sparked a bit of controversy. One of its marketing images was edited due to allegedly displaying what could be considered an offensive gesture.

The regional online Apple Store for South Korea looks a lot like others around the world. However, according to ITHome, one image showing the thin profile of the iPad mini has had its hand removed from view.

The hand itself exists on other Apple regional websites, but is removed from view just in South Korea.

A mean-spirited gesture

The hand is palm-up, with the thumb and forefinger extended and gripping onto one end of the iPad mini from the right-hand side.

As it is, in most of the world this would be considered a fairly adequate way to show the iPad mini's thin size while still holding onto it. In South Korea, this gesture can be considered offensive to some observers.

In short, some take the hand gesture to be insulting the size of a man's manhood. For some online communities, it is used as a symbol for misandry.

It isn't a gesture that most people would take offense to, but it only needs a small and vocal audience to cause trouble.

The controversy over the so-called "C" gesture reached its height in 2023, reports the Korea Times, after a video produced for the Nexon game MapleStory included a similar gesture.

Online denizens thought it was used on purpose as a pro-feminist message.

As usual for the Internet, users started to try and find other instances of characters in Nexon's marketing imagery for other games to stoke the controversy.

The affair resulted in a public apology from the developers, as well as the promise of an investigation and the taking down of all related videos.

Cultural sensitivity

This is also not the only time Apple has avoided using the gesture on its website, specifically in South Korea. Imagery for the iPhone Air also lacks the fingers at the top of the regional page, while still appearing in other versions.

For a major multinational like Apple, it has to be mindful of cultural differences across multiple borders. What may be considered perfectly fine in one country may not be in another.

It's a challenge to keep up, but in this instance, Apple seems to have made the change preemptively rather than reactively, and without harming the meaning of the imagery either.

At least Apple worked the issue out beforehand. The last thing it needed was another penis-finger billboard situation on its hands.

items.title: iPhone Duo hinge maker denies blame for screen failures
items.content_html:
An Apple supplier insists that its components aren't the cause of hinge failures that break the screen of the iPhone Duo, as the social media fallout over the fault rolls on.

Following the release of the iPhone Duo, there have been reports of screen breakages, with quite a few highlighting a very common point of failure for the hinge. In an attempt to get ahead of the story, part of Apple's supply chain claims that its components are not the problem.

A statement from Fine M-Tec released on October 26 denies that its components cause the screen damage, reports The Elec. It also urges everyone to avoid a witch hunt for someone to blame until the real cause has been uncovered.

"The quality issues recently reported in certain products were not caused by defects in components supplied by our company," Fine M-Tec insists, without directly mentioning Apple. The supplier adds that it is also considering legal action against anyone making claims about its components without the issue being validated.

Fine M-Tec is a manufacturer of internal hinges and metal plates that are used to support foldable OLED displays. The intention of the plates are to help protect the panel from the stress of folding and unfolding.

The company is known as a supplier of components in that field to Samsung Display, and therefore is part of the foldable smartphone supply chain.

Oh Snap

Consumers and product testers of the destructive variety have repeatedly demonstrated in video and photographs that a fault can occur on the center line. While this is not exceptional on its own, there is a pattern of a horizontal line appearing at one particular point along the center of the display, which goes off to one side.

A closer examination and disassembly of the iPhone Duo has already identified a possible suspect, in the form of a flat element snapping into two pieces during the folding and unfolding process.

This takes place close to the middle of the display, where a small support plate comes close to other elements, including an interconnecting cable between the two halves.

Following the blowing up of the screen cracking issue, Apple has made a brief statement acknowledging it is aware, and for users to contact AppleCare for a replacement.

While it is unclear how many devices are affected, it isn't believed to be a widespread problem for Apple.

After speaking to staff members at 20 Genius Bars that AppleInsider trusts, there have only been four impacted iPhone Duo units returned so far as of October 26. Polling will continue after US stores open.

items.title: It's back - the glowing Apple logo makes a return on MacBook Pro at last
items.content_html:
The first MacBook Pro that lacked Apple's iconic backlit logo was released in 2016. A decade later, it's back.

For a long time, the thing about the lit Apple logo on the lid of its portables was that it was the wrong way around. It was positioned for the user to see as they opened the lid, while it was then upside down for anyone passing by.

Never one to miss out on good advertising, Apple flipped that logo around. To this day its glowing symbol shines out from concert stages around the world.

It just also tells you how long it is since those concert musicians updated. Because the very first Apple laptop to eschew the lit logo was the 2015 12-inch MacBook, and then the first MacBook Pro was in 2016.

What it was

It was more symbolic than anything technical. Apple just cut out a hole in the shape of its logo and stuck some translucent plastic in there. Since the lid contained the backlighting for the front display, there was enough illumination to spare that this logo had a warmly welcoming glow.

But it was still an extra layer that room had to be found for. As the MacBook Pro got ever more thin and light, the thinness won and the light lost. Shortly after that first 2016 MacBook Pro lost its lit logo, they all did.

But it's back

Curiously, one of the features of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR models is that they are thinner. The screen, specifically, is significantly thinner enough to be called out by Apple as a selling point.

First look at the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and yes the Apple Logo on the lid lights up again! https://t.co/e5mEkGyXXx

— Rich DeMuro (@richontech) October 28, 2026

It's a feature of Apple using the tandem OLED display which dispenses with the usual backlight and extra layers of screen. Those layers made the screen clear, but they also meant more power was needed to make the display viewable.

And of course more layers meant more width. So by switching to tandem OLED, Apple has saved a quite remarkable amount of space. On the new 14-inch model, the screen is half a millimeter thinner, while on the 16-inch, it's almost a millimeter.

Despite achieving that thinness, Apple has chosen to reinstate the famous backlit logo. Perhaps it's again a function of the lit screen bleeding through, perhaps it was possible to do it without adding as thick a piece of translucent plastic and relying on the LED backlight as before.

But whatever the reason and however it was done, Apple has quietly called back to its distinctive past. It will now again be shining out from stages, and there will again be whole seas of lit Apple logos in classrooms and at events.

It wasn't the end of the world when the logo went, but if you were a longtime Mac user, you did feel it. So this is a good day.

And since the logo vanished under Tim Cook's watch, you have to wonder whether it's back because of John Ternus. He's not been CEO for very long, but he has been deeply embedded in the company's design teams for most of his time with the company.

items.title: Mac Studio M5 Ultra 512GB RAM upgrade costs $15,500 on its own
items.content_html:
Months after Apple launched the latest Mac Studio, it is finally taking orders for one more configuration, the 512GB RAM M5 Ultra. It's extremely costly.

Apple launched the M5 Ultra and M5 Max editions of the Mac Studio in August 2026, but revealed in barely a footnote that there was one configuration coming later. Even as Apple was saying that the Mac Studio could be configured to have 512GB RAM, it actually couldn't. Until now.

As of now, pre-orders are open for what could be the best Mac ever made. It's the M5 Ultra Mac Studio, and it can now come with 96GB RAM and all the way up to 512GB.

The base M5 Ultra comes with 96GB RAM, 30-core CPU, and 64-core GPU, plus 1TB storage, for $5,499. The M5 Ultra edition can also be bought with a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU for a further $1,300.

Upgrading the storage from 1TB to the maximum 16TB costs an additional $7,500. Only the 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU model can take 512GB of RAM.

So in August 2026 when the M5 Ultra model was announced, it was possible to spend up to $18,299 on one. Now Apple has made the most powerful Mac ever cost $29,799.

Don't expect this one to sell out as quickly as the iPhone Duo. But if you need this performance, you don't want to wait any longer than you already have.

The first pre-orders for this configuration will arrive on December 3.

items.title: Russia orders Apple to surrender users' messages on demand
items.content_html:
Apple and Microsoft have been added to a Russian state surveillance registry, requiring them to hand over users' text, video and audio messages without a legal process, and by request.

Multiple firms and apps are already on this same list, including WhatsApp and Telegram, so it's not clear why it has taken until now for Apple to be added. It's a continuation of the country's moves to control users' messages, though, as it follows Russia's blocking of FaceTime in 2025.

According to Bloomberg, Apple and Microsoft were added to this registry of "organizers of information dissemination" on October 2, 2026. The registry is operated by the country's state media watchdog, Roskomnadzor, which previously forced Apple to remove VPN apps from the App Store.

Now that Apple is on this registry, Russian law requires it to store local users' correspondence for up to three years. That data must be stored on servers within Russia, and it must be turned over to the country's security services as required.

Neither Apple nor Microsoft has yet commented publicly on the new requirements. Apple does observe the law in its international markets, but it has also removed features if it disagrees with those laws.

So when the UK ordered unwarranted access to user data in 2025, Apple disabled its Advanced Data Protection feature solely in that country. Plus it continues to not offer many features, and now also the HomeView, in the EU because of disputes over regulatory conditions.

Russia's demands on Apple and others

Back in 2022, Russian authorities fined Apple for not storing iCloud data on local servers. In that same year, Russia also made a legal requirement that major technology companies establish offices in the country.

Consequently, Apple opened an office in Moscow in February 2022.

Apple in Russia

Despite setting up that office, Apple has never had any Apple Stores in Russia. It also stopped online sales in the country in 2022 at the start of the attacks on Ukraine.

But Apple devices have been sold through third-party resellers for decades, and its services remained available to Russian subscribers until early 2026. That was at least in part because services such as the App Store are a grey area legally.

If a Russian iPhone user, for instance, subscribes to a Russian app, that in theory has nothing to do with Apple. But Apple runs the App Store and takes income from it.

So in March 2026, Apple reported itself to regulators. Since all non-US Apple sales are the responsibility of Apple Ireland, it was that division that reported the issue, and did so to UK regulators.

The UK ruled that Apple had breached sanctions against Russia "on the balance of probabilities." It fined Apple, and Apple ceased allowing such subscriptions to continue.

items.title: How macOS is changing on touchscreens beyond Sidecar, but only a bit
items.content_html:
Apple didn't just put a touchscreen on the MacBook Pro, it made some minor macOS changes to buttons and menus to accommodate your fingers. Here's where they are so far, and what apps will get them first.

The company introduced the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display at its "Pro and tell" event in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28. The new models start at $2,899 and $3,399, respectively, with preorders open now and availability beginning November 6.

The laptops run macOS 27 and retain the traditional keyboard and trackpad. Apple has added touchscreen support without replacing the desktop interface that Mac users already know.

One of the clearest changes involves the red, yellow and green buttons at the top-left corner of Mac windows. In its hands-on report, The Verge found that the buttons grow larger when touched, making them easier to select with a finger. A short video posted by Neil Cybart shows the same behavior, although the buttons appear to respond with a slight delay.

A closer look at how window controls in macOS respond to touch. https://t.co/OT8NIiVM4S

— Neil Cybart (@neilcybart) October 28, 2026

The adjustment addresses a practical problem with touchscreen laptops. Controls designed for a precise mouse pointer aren't always large enough to tap comfortably.

Apple's announcement also describes familiar gestures, including swiping to scroll, pinching to zoom and dragging slides between presentations. Users can double-tap a window to fill the screen or flick it into a tiled position.

macOS 27.2 adds more touch-specific controls

Additional interface changes have appeared in macOS 27.2 beta testing, although they haven't all been independently demonstrated on the new MacBook Pro. Some demonstrations use Sidecar, which lets an iPad act as a Mac display.

Apple introduced direct finger control for Sidecar in macOS 27, allowing users to navigate Mac apps on an iPad without an Apple Pencil, as hands-on testing showed in June.

The company's developer guidance confirms that macOS 27 handles Sidecar touch input through gesture recognizers. The capability provides a way to test touch interactions on a Mac without using the new laptop.

In Safari 27.2, tabs lift and enlarge when users drag them to change their order. X user pdfu demonstrated that pressing and holding a tab also opens a touch-specific context menu that omits the usual "Ask Siri" option.

Finder makes a smaller but useful adjustment. Its Edit Tags menu adds more spacing between items when opened with a finger, creating larger targets without permanently changing the menu's compact appearance.

Calendar has another adaptation in macOS 27.2. Events display circular resize handles during touch interaction, giving users a larger area to grab when changing an event's duration.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

None of those adjustments requires macOS to adopt an iPad-style layout. Instead, individual controls respond differently depending on how users interact with them.

The beta findings show that Apple is developing touch-specific interface changes beyond basic gestures. However, they don't confirm which changes will be available on the new MacBook Pro when it ships Nov. 6.

Touch support goes beyond Apple's apps

Apple says many existing Mac apps will support touch immediately because macOS converts finger taps into mouse clicks. The conversion provides basic touch compatibility, but it doesn't make every app's interface easier to navigate with a finger.

Developers can add more advanced touch features using Apple's updated gesture APIs. The APIs let apps recognize finger gestures directly instead of relying entirely on simulated mouse clicks.

Apple's creative software provides examples of what more specialized support looks like. Logic Pro will offer a multitouch software keyboard and on-screen instrument pads, while Final Cut Pro will let editors mark ranges, move clips and pinch to zoom in on a cut.

Pixelmator Pro will also support direct interaction with images, including drawing, painting and selecting content on the display. Apple says the related Creator Studio updates will arrive in November.

Third-party developers are preparing touch features as well. Apple's announcement names Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Adobe Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender and other professional apps, with the listed software updates expected later in 2026.

Apps that accept finger taps won't necessarily offer larger controls or multitouch features designed for the new display.

Apple has also brought Dynamic Island to the MacBook Pro, creating a touch-enabled area for Live Activities, music controls and other information. Users can tap to pause a song or accept an AirDrop request without opening another window.

Spotlight and Siri AI are part of Apple's plans for Dynamic Island, although their availability has conditions. Spotlight moves there only when Siri AI is available and enabled, and Siri AI is currently in beta in macOS 27.2.

Apple has made macOS more touch-friendly without abandoning its familiar desktop layout. It's still unclear how consistently the changes will work across third-party apps when the touchscreen MacBook Pro reaches customers.

items.title: The global memory crisis will annoy everyone until 2030 at least
items.content_html:
The memory crisis isn't going to be solved before 2030, and there's a new shortage brewing that's just going to make things worse and more expensive.

Manufacturers and consumers are already dealing with the effects of high memory demand caused primarily through AI data center and infrastructure buildouts. Now, it seems that the problem will be affecting more components, and for years longer than anyone really expected.

In its Q3 financial results released on Wednesday, memory maker SK Hynix claims it achieved revenues of 104 trillion won ($77 billion) and a net profit of 39.7 trillion won ($29 billion), thanks to record sales.

However, the company is also aware that its high revenue has a backdrop of the memory supply shortage. "AI-driven productivity gains" has helped lead to greater AI adoption, resulting in more investment in infrastructure.

With the prospect of AI data center growth continuing to be steady for the foreseeable future, SK Hynix also points out a supply problem. In its assessment, supplies are not keeping up with the growth of the market.

There's also the technical difficulty of "leading-edge processes" as well as the lengthy construction time to make new manufacturing facilities to consider. SK Hynix expects that demand for memory will continue to exceed supply through 2030.

An expanded problem

While the prospect of waiting years for memory prices to stabilize or even start to return to normal is a bad one, it's not the only issue AI is causing.

According to Nikkei Asia, there's another supply constraint that's affecting electronics producers. Printed circuit boards are in short supply too.

Just like consumer computers and enterprise servers, AI infrastructure relies on printed circuit boards (PCBs) to plug everything into and to get the components working together.

AI server makers have their own custom motherboards, made to be more efficient and to cope with the needs of AI processing. This puts a strain on the PCB market, affecting practically anyone needing a circuit board.

PC manufacturers such as HP and Dell are already locking in with suppliers early, so they can avoid the supply capacity limits that have plagued the memory industry. In turn, this will impact the cost of boards across the industry.

Higher prices, for longer

Once again, this is a big problem for consumers in general, including Apple device users. Like other PC and electronics manufacturers, Apple has to compete in the same market, with very similar constraints.

Apple does have the benefit of its sheer size and the scale of its supply chain operations. It too will use its expertise to secure components long in advance, just as it did to insulate consumers from memory price rises.

However, just like the memory problem, this is something Apple cannot maintain in the long term. Eventually, if prices rise even more, they will be passed down to consumers, increasing the cost of future iPhones and Macs.

It was already expected that the RAM supply crisis would get worse before it gets better. While memory producers fight to build out facilities as fast as they can, it's still a multi-year process that will take a very long time.

Short of a major event cutting AI's appetite for memory and circuit boards, we face quite a few years of painful product pricing.

items.title: As expected, you're going to pay a lot if you want a touchscreen MacBook Pro
items.content_html:
Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro reportedly carries a $400 premium, with a starting price of $2,899.

Apple is expected to introduce 14-inch and 16-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro models on Wednesday as premium additions to the lineup. The existing non-touchscreen models will remain available alongside them.

According to Bloomberg's sources, Apple mulled over a $2,899 starting price for the 14-inch model with an M5 Pro chip. That would make it $400 more expensive than the current 14-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro.

The current 16-inch MacBook Pro starts at $2,999 without a touchscreen. A matching $400 increase would situate the new model at $3,399.

At $2,899, the 14-inch model would have the highest starting price of any new MacBook Pro. That comes in at $700 more than the 14-inch and 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro models before Apple's mid-year price hikes.

The new touchscreen MacBooks will feature OLED XDR displays and a Dynamic Island, while retaining the current lineup's general appearance. They'll also have thinner display borders, slightly slimmer bodies, and weigh less.

Apple has also redesigned the hinge to keep the screen steady during touch input. The cooling system has been redesigned, reducing weight and improving airflow through the hinge.

The company has updated macOS Golden Gate to support touch, including dial-like menus that appear around a user's finger. The keyboard and trackpad will remain the primary input methods.

Apple plans to begin taking preorders on Wednesday, with sales potentially starting on November 6. That would match the release date for the updated iPad mini, M6 MacBook Pro, and M6 iMac announced earlier this week.

The first touchscreen MacBook Pros will likely feature the M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, skipping the M6 chip. Bloomberg says that Apple is also developing M7 Pro and M7 Max versions for the fall of 2027.

items.title: M6 vs M4: How two years and two chip generations change Apple Silicon
items.content_html:
Owners of M4 Macs may feel the temptation to upgrade to the M6 Mac mini, MacBook Pro, or iMac. Here's what to expect with the jump to Apple's newest silicon.

In August 2026, Apple introduced the M6 as its new entry-level chip, as well as the M6 generation itself. Brought out with the Mac mini, the M6 was framed by Apple as a way to benefit more from AI, with changes that made it an ideal chip for machine learning workloads.

The introduction took place just over two years after Apple launched its first M4 chip in the iPad Pro. The M6 is also a two-generation jump for some models, such as the Mac mini, which skipped the base M5 chip completely.

With Apple bringing out more hardware using M6, more consumers are going to look at the new hardware and seriously consider upgrading from their M4 equivalents.

This is the breakdown of what Apple's M6 chip provides, and how it is different from the M4.

M6 vs M4: Processes and transistors

The M6 and M4 are made by Apple's usual chip foundry partner, TSMC. However, they are made using two different processes.

The M4 was made using a 3-nanometer process, while the M6 uses a 2-nanometer version.

There are usually quite a few benefits for a so-called die shrink, with the first being density. You can fit more transistors in a smaller process level than a larger one, simply because everything is much smaller.

When it comes to transistors, TSMC was able to squeeze 46 billion onto the M6 die. The M4, meanwhile, has just over half that figure at 28 billion transistors.

M6 vs M4: Die shrinks let you fit transistors more densely.

The more transistors on a chip, the more potential calculations and processes it can perform.

The smaller dies can also get advantages in other areas, such as requiring less power for processing. Heat dissipation is also improved on smaller processes.

The die shrink means that the M6 can run cooler and with less energy than the M4 on comparable workloads.

M6 vs M4: Cores and clock speeds

Modern processors don't just have multiple cores, but multiple core types, too. Cores at different clock speeds can help a system better manage power in relation to performance needs.

A high-performance core may not be used while a system is idling, leaving background work for lower-powered efficiency cores to do. When it comes to completing a task, those performance cores come into play.

The M4 has ten cores in Macs, consisting of four performance cores, and six efficiency cores. A nine-core CPU was also available in the iPad Pro, with three performance cores.

The performance cores are clocked at 4.4GHz, while the efficiency cores run at 2.85GHz.

When it comes to the M6, Apple decided to add a new core type to the equation. Alongside the four performance and six efficiency cores, there were a pair of "super" cores that perform at an even higher level.

In the first M6 release, this meant the super cores ran at 4.79GHz, the performance cores at 4.5GHz, and the efficiency cores at 2.94GHz.

Not only does the M6 run at faster clock rates per-core overall, but there's also the benefit of having two extra cores available.

M6 vs M4: Memory

One of the few advantages the M4 has over the M6 is memory quantity support, at least in theory.

The M4 has been used in devices with configurations between 8GB and 32GB of memory, while the M6 goes from 16GB to 32GB allocations.

The reason for this is that there were iPad Pro models with M4 that had just 8GB of memory. There hasn't been an M6 device with less than 16GB.

M6 vs M4: M6 arrived with the Mac mini. There's not been an M6 iPad Pro yet, at the time of reporting.

That said, the M6 still wins out when it comes to bandwidth.

The M4 has a memory bandwidth maximum of 120GB/s. That's dwarfed by the M6, which goes to 170GB/s.

Memory bandwidth is essential, since Apple relies on using Unified Memory. The same memory is used by the CPU, GPU, and other components to minimize data duplication, which is common when separate pools of memory are being used.

M6 vs M4: Graphics and the Neural Engine

While in previous years, we would separate the GPU and the Neural Engine, changes in Apple's hardware landscape means they should be discussed together.

First, the Neural Engine in the M4 has 16 cores, as is tradition, with the capability of performing up to 38 trillion operations per second.

By comparison, the Neural Engine in the M6 is a "Dual 16-core" version. This means it has 32 cores to play with, double that of the M4.

On the GPU side, the M4 has a few configurations depending on the device, at eight, nine, or ten cores. The GPU also has hardware-accelerated ray-tracing, which helps with rendering graphics.

The M6, meanwhile, has a 12-core GPU in its base configuration. The newer GPUs are always declared as being faster than the previous generations, but the M6 has one more advantage over the M4.

The M6 GPU cores have Neural Accelerators in each core. Introduced with the M5, they handle matrix-multiplication operations, which are a bedrock of processing AI and large language models (LLMs).

While the M6 benefits from double the Neural Engine cores for a start, the GPU's Neural Accelerators gives it a massive advantage when it comes to AI processing in general.

That makes the M6 a quite desirable chip for those working in AI.

M6 vs M4: Benchmarks

A good way to demonstrate the performance difference between the M4 and M6 chips is by benchmarking them on the same sort of hardware. Since the Mac mini exists in both M4 and M6 variants, it's an ideal vehicle for this.

M6 vs M4: Geekbench single-core

Under Geekbench 7's listings, the M4 Mac mini manages a single-core score of 3,277. The super core of the M6 Mac mini helps push it further, right up to 4,002, a 22% improvement.

M6 vs M4: Geekbench multi-core

The multi-core score of the M4 Mac mini is decent, with the ten cores managing 15,304 when working together. However, the faster cores and the increased count in the M6 Mac mini reach 21,881, over 42% better.

M6 vs M4: Geekbench Metal

Under Metal, there's a similar gulf of performance. The M4's 54,227 is heavily beaten by the 89,375 of the M6, a 64% improvement.

M6 vs M4: Two generations of improvement

Looking at the M6 against the M4 was always going to be a performance bloodbath. There is a lot of change that happens between two chip generations, with every small alteration helping to grow the gap.

The M6 certainly is an AI-forward chip, with masses of graphical performance aiding the double-sized Neural Engine. And then there's the CPU core improvements and the additional two Super cores to account for, too.

It's easy to see how much of an improvement the M6 has, which directly translates into everyday tasks. You can certainly see where Apple is going with its future Apple Silicon efforts.

That all said, the M4 is still very capable. It's not what you would consider slow, but the M6 is helping show its age a bit.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Design, weight, size

The MacBook Pro has a very well-defined design, namely Apple's aluminum slab aesthetic. It's quite fond of its designs, and doesn't like to change them that much if it can help it.

The M5 MacBook Pro measures 12.31 inches long by 8.71 inches wide, just like the M4 version. Its thickness of 0.61 inches was also identical, and keeps the design fairly thin for a notebook.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Closed, from the front, the M6 is just as thin as the M5 version. - Image Credit: Apple

The only change introduced during the M5 launch was a new Space Black colorway replacing Grey alongside Silver.

As usual for a spec-bump update, the footprint of the M6 version is exactly the same size, as well as thickness.

For weight, there's also no real difference here. The M5 MacBook Pro was 3.4 pounds, which the M6 also matches.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Display

While there is the considerable prospect of an OLED display on the horizon, it is evident that Apple still wants to sell its current MacBook display tech to consumers.

The M5 reused the M4 model's display, meaning it has a 14.2-inch screen with a resolution of 3,024 by 1,964. The pixel density of 254 pixels per inch is typical of Apple's MacBook lineup.

The XDR screen benefited from mini LED backlighting, enabling a million-to-one contrast ratio. Brightness hit 1,000 nits for SDR content, 1,600 nits at a peak for HDR content.

The M5 model also supported a billion colors, Wide Color (P3) gamut, and True Tone. ProMotion enabled refresh rates to adapt, going as high as 120 Hz.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Front view. - Image Credit: Apple

Unsurprisingly, all of this is mirrored in the M6 MacBook Pro, too.

That also includes the dreaded notch, located at the top of the screen and holding a camera. The M5 introduced an optional Nano-texture coating to minimize glare, which the M6 retains.

For external display support, the M5 was able to handle two 6K-resolution 60Hz displays using Thunderbolt. Using the HDMI, you could run an 8K 60Hz display, or a 4K one at 240Hz.

The M6 can do the same thing with external displays.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Performance

The M5 in the previous 14-inch MacBook Pro had ten CPU cores, consisting of four super cores and six efficiency cores. It was joined by a 16-core Neural Engine, a 10-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, and a Media Engine.

The switch to the M6 brings many performance-related changes. Starting with the CPU, which is a 12-core version, with the usual claims of speed improvements over the previous generation.

The core mix this time is described as two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: The M6 has a performance bump on the M5. - Image Credit: Apple

The Neural Engine is back again, but this time it's a "Dual 16-core" version, meaning it has 32 cores to play with. You can add on top of that the Neural Accelerators in the 12-core GPU, as well as the usual Media Engine for hardware-accelerated video encoding and decoding.

Then there's memory bandwidth. For the M5, there was 153GB/s available, but this has been increased to 170GB/s in the M6.

When it comes to performance, Apple claims the M6 model has 1.3 times the render performance in Blender than the M5, 1.2 times faster image processing in Affinity, and 1.3 times faster Xcode code compilation. For the growing AI processing needs of its audience, there's a 1.3 times improvement too.

We can't immediately benchmark the M6 MacBook Pro just yet. However, we can use the M6 Mac mini to give some idea of what to expect in terms of performance gains.

It's not going to be an exact match for the MacBook Pro due to various factors, such as thermal management differences. Even so, it will still provide a ballpark figure.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Single-core benchmarks

For single-core performance in Geekbench 7's listings, the M5 MacBook Pro achieves a pretty good 3,647. The M6 Mac mini, however, does 9.7% better at 4,002.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Multi-core benchmarks

The multi-core benchmark is less tight, with the 17,955 of the M5 beaten by the M6's 21,881. That's a 22% margin that can be partially explained by the extra two cores in the M6.

Lastly, graphics, with the M5 MacBook Pro's score of 72,726 still pretty respectable. However, the 89,375 of the M6 Mac mini is a 23% improvement again.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Metal benchmarks

We know there will be a performance improvement going from the M5 to the M6, as is usual for a new generation. While there's a bit of a jump from each, it's not a bad performance for the M5 at all.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Camera and Audio

The notch of the M5 14-inch MacBook Pro included an improved 12MP Center Stage camera. As the name implied, the camera would reframe the shot so the subject was in the middle, making it extremely handy for video calls.

That 1080p video feed, boosted by an advanced image signal processor, also had Desk View, which faked a top-down view of the desk.

Evidently, Apple decided this worked well enough not to change. It's the same camera in the M6 version.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: The ports, like the rest of the design, are unchanged. - Image Credit: Apple

For audio, the M5 and the M6 both use a high-fidelity six-speaker sound system with force-cancelling woofers. There was also Spatial Audio support for Dolby Atmos content, both through speakers and with AirPods using Spatial Audio with dynamic head tracking.

The M5 had a headphone jack capable of working with high-impedance headphones, making it great for audiophiles. This too is maintained for the M6 model.

When it comes to audio recording, the M5 MacBook Pro used an array of three "studio-quality" microphones with a high signal-to-noise ratio and directional beamforming. These persist in the M6 with the same specifications.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Storage, connectivity, power

The M5 MacBook Pro included 512GB of storage at its lowest, with upgrade options for 1TB, 2TB, and 4TB. In March 2026, it cut the 512GB option, leaving the 1TB to 4TB range intact.

For M6, Apple's maintaining this later range, with the lowest capacity at 1TB.

On the physical connectivity side, there are three Thunderbolt 4 ports on both models, along with HDMI and an SDXC memory card slot, as well as the headphone jack. MagSafe 3 is also present for charging duties on both models.

14" MacBook Pro M5

Apple's 2025 14-inch MacBook Pro has an M5 chip and is equipped with three Thunderbolt 4 ports.
Buy at Amazon
Buy at B&H
Buy at Expercom

The wireless connectivity on the M5 14-inch MacBook Pro consisted of Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 for accessories. Under the M6, these have been upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, though those will only really be beneficial if you have similarly-supportive accessories or wireless network infrastructure.

When it comes to power, the M5 model had a 72.4-watt-hour lithium-polymer battery. Apple claimed it could last for up to 24 hours of video streaming and up to 16 hours of wireless web access.

This hasn't changed at all with the M6.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Pricing

The base 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 launched at $1,599, but the global memory crisis had other ideas. The price for the base model rose to $1,999, with the Standard Display, M5 chip, 16GB of unified memory, and 1TB of storage.

Increasing the memory to 24GB cost $200, rising by another $200 for the 32GB maximum. If you wanted more storage, the upgrade to 2TB was $500, while 4TB was another $1,000 on top of that.

The included 70W USB-C adapter could also be upgraded to a 96W version for just $20, while Nano-texture was $150.

The new M6 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 with the Standard Display, 16GB of memory, and 1TB of storage.

The memory upgrade jumps are again $200 to 24GB and $200 more to 32GB. Likewise, going to 2TB of storage is a $500 fee, and 4TB another $1,000 beyond that.

The charger upgrade is once more $20, with Nano-texture a $150 upgrade.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: Which to buy?

When it comes to buying a base MacBook Pro from Apple directly, you don't really have much choice in the matter. You're stuck with whatever the newest chip is, which in this case is the M6.

It's also a spec-bump update through and through, with very few internal changes instead of anything major and exterior. That puts the M6 model into the bracket of being aimed at consumers who absolutely need to upgrade, or are buying their first MacBook Pro.

M6 MacBook Pro vs M5 MacBook Pro: It's faster and better, but no OLED yet. - Image Credit: Apple

There is no realistic reason to upgrade from the M5 to the M6. Things like the Neural Accelerators helped justify people upgrading to the M5, but this time it's a more muted jump up.

It also doesn't help the M6 that it's in the shadow of a rumored launch of an OLED MacBook Pro. For people wanting a serious upgrade from the M5 MacBook Pro, that is what they will be watching out for, not a small upgrade.

That all said, the M6 has still earned its place as being a pretty good entry-level MacBook Pro, for those who want something a little meatier than a MacBook Air.

Where to buy Apple's M6 14-inch MacBook Pro and M5 14-inch MacBook Pro

Apple's new M6 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 and can be purchased at B&H Photo and Amazon.

The closeout M5 14-inch MacBook Pro, meanwhile, is currently on sale from $1,839 at Amazon. A full rundown of the deals and availability can be found in our M5 14-inch MacBook Pro Price Guide.

items.title: Up to 350,000 Macs exposed by a forgotten Popcorn Time updater
items.content_html:
An abandoned Popcorn Time updater left up to 350,000 Macs vulnerable to remote takeover, giving potential attackers a way to execute malicious code with full system privileges.

Security researchers at Eye Research detailed the discovery in an October 22, 2026, research report about Operation IXIM. The vulnerability affected Time4Popcorn, an abandoned fork of the popular BitTorrent streaming application that continued circulating under the Popcorn Time name after the original project shut down in 2014.

Some users had stopped using Popcorn Time, but its updater kept running. Eye Research discovered attackers could hijack it to install malware and intervened between November 2025 and March 2026.

How a forgotten updater exposed hundreds of thousands of Macs

The investigation began when Eye Research discovered an updater contacting an abandoned domain from a customer's Windows computer. Researchers registered the domain and found that approximately 50 requests were arriving every second from devices still running the software.

On macOS, the vulnerable component was a privileged helper called PT.updd, which launched automatically when the computer started. Like other macOS background services, the updater could run independently of the application itself, even when its owner wasn't actively using Popcorn Time.

The updater contacted its servers over unencrypted HTTP connections and accepted downloaded code without verifying its digital signature. On Macs, that code ran with root privileges, giving an attacker the ability to execute commands with the highest level of system access.

Anyone controlling one of the abandoned update domains, or capable of manipulating the network traffic, could potentially exploit the mechanism. The vulnerability was assigned CVE-2026-30612, although Eye Research didn't establish that criminals had already exploited it.

"We mapped a sample of the IP addresses using kepler.gl and they were everywhere." Image credit: Eye Research

Determining how many Macs were affected proved difficult. Researchers initially recorded approximately 1.7 million unique Mac identifiers, but later discovered that changes to a computer's hostname or network hardware addresses could cause the same machine to appear multiple times.

Eye Research revised its estimate to between 250,000 and 350,000 Macs. The company also estimated that approximately 2.5 million to 3 million Windows PCs had contacted the affected update infrastructure, although those figures aren't a verified count of individual devices.

Researchers used the vulnerability to disable the updater

With the original developers gone and no official patch available, Eye Research decided to use the vulnerable update mechanism to protect affected computers. The researchers developed a small update that disabled the background service responsible for checking for new software.

On Macs, the update ran a shell command that stopped the launch daemon responsible for starting PT.updd. The intervention didn't remove the application itself, and Eye Research said its repair was designed to leave other software and files untouched.

The approach raised legal and ethical questions because researchers were executing code on computers without their owners' explicit permission. Eye Research said it consulted its legal team and conducted extensive testing before deploying the update more widely.

The operation also encountered an unexpected obstacle involving antivirus software. On Windows, 11 security vendors initially detected the repair tool as malicious because it disabled an existing service, prompting researchers to modify their code to avoid those detections.

By December 2025, Eye Research reported deploying the update to more than a million systems. The campaign ultimately distributed more than 2 million update downloads, although that figure doesn't necessarily represent 2 million unique computers or confirmed successful repairs.

By March 1, 2026, the company was still delivering approximately 5,000 updates daily, representing a reported 98% decrease from earlier volumes. Eye Research subsequently ended the deployment and transferred 15 domains it controlled to the nonprofit Shadowserver Foundation in late March.

"A bit of debugging led us to this snippet of the code that was generating the hid." Image credit: Eye Research

The researchers couldn't obtain every domain associated with the abandoned software, leaving some update infrastructure outside their control. Their intervention substantially reduced the apparent exposure, but it doesn't guarantee that every vulnerable Mac received the repair.

Disabling the updater doesn't make Popcorn Time safe

Eye Research also discovered serious vulnerabilities in the main application that weren't addressed by the emergency update. The affected Time4Popcorn software uses a browser engine dating to 2014, with its security sandbox disabled.

The app loads JavaScript over unencrypted connections from domains its original developers no longer maintain. Researchers showed that malicious JavaScript could run programs on Windows, but they didn't demonstrate the same attack on macOS.

Disabling the vulnerable updater addressed only one security risk. The outdated Popcorn Time application could still expose users to malicious content and attacks that manipulate network traffic.

Abandoned software can remain a security risk long after developers stop supporting it. Even when nobody opens the application, privileged background processes can keep running without security updates.

How to remove Popcorn Time and protect your Mac

Mac users who installed the Time4Popcorn version of Popcorn Time should remove it, even if they haven't opened the app in years. Eye Research recommends a complete uninstall because disabling the updater doesn't fix the app's other security vulnerabilities.

Deleting apps from the Applications folder doesn't necessarily remove associated background services. Users can check for the vulnerable Mac updater by opening Finder, selecting Go > Go to Folder, and entering /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/ to look for a file named PT.updd.

The associated launch daemon is located at /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist. Eye Research's security advisory provides the specific Terminal command needed to disable the service if it's still present.

Mac owners should also keep macOS updated and maintain Apple's built-in malware protections. However, operating system security updates won't correct vulnerabilities in an abandoned third-party application.

The findings specifically concern the older Time4Popcorn fork and don't apply to a separate project that began using the Popcorn Time name in 2025.

items.title: Slight 14-inch MacBook Pro refresh adds M6 AI power, Wi-Fi 7
items.content_html:
The lower-end 14-inch MacBook Pro got an update on Tuesday, with the model getting better wireless networking, and most importantly, more power with the M6 processor.

It's not the flashiest of upgrades, nor is there an associated enclosure re-design. But, in the middle of a week of upgrades, Apple announced the new model in a press release.

There's still no M6 Pro or M6 Max processor, and those are not expected soon, if ever. However, the "entry level" MacBook Pro is getting the M6 chip that debuted in the Mac mini.

The M6 processor here has 12 processing cores broken down into two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores. The M6 here also has 12 GPU cores.

It comes standard with 16GB of RAM. Thunderbolt 4 remains.

Apple also says that the battery life has been extended to up to 14 hours of use.

Along with that, Apple's N1 chip is included. That incorporates Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. And, as before, Apple claims that improves performance and reliability of AirDrop and other wireless connectivity features.

"The 14-inch MacBook Pro is the pro laptop of choice for a wide range of users — from college students, to business professionals across every industry, to multidisciplinary creators doing it all on one device," said Shelly Goldberg, Apple's vice president of Hardware Engineering. "With the powerful M6 chip, we're taking performance to the next level, with a boost in CPU speed and graphics and even more powerful capabilities for on-device AI. With its amazing battery life, remarkable Liquid Retina XDR display, and even faster connectivity, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 delivers a fantastic combination of performance, capability, and value."

Apple's performance testing

The company also has something to say about performance versus prior generations. Take these with a grain of salt, as always.

  • Up to 13x faster time to first token performance for LLM prompt processing compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
  • Up to 11.7x faster render performance with ray tracing in Blender compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
  • Up to 3.3x faster image-processing performance in Affinity compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.2x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
  • Up to 2.5x faster project build performance when compiling code in Xcode compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.

Preorder timing and cost

Prices start at $1999 with the M6, 1TB of storage, and 16GB of RAM. There is only one M6 chip to pick from, but with 32GB of RAM and a 4TB SSD, the new model sells for $3899.

Preorders start on October 28, with models expected to arrive on November 6.

items.title: MotionVFX, AI tools feature in Apple Creator Studio's latest update
items.content_html:
Apple Creator Studio has more AI-based updates, with the biggest change being the inclusion of MotionVFX plug-ins and templates.

Apple has been steadily making updates to the Apple Creator Studio, including one in September taking advantage of the new iPhone 18 Pro camera. Its latest update is, however, more AI-focused.

The main change is the inclusion of MotionVFX directly into Final Cut Pro for Mac. The addition brings with it thousands of templates, graphics, titles, and transitions.

There are also tools to help with rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading.

Cross-app workflows have also been improved, with editors now able to open images from their Final Cut Pro timeline directly in Pixelmator Pro without reimporting. There's also advanced image generation, more keyframe easing options, and 23 new transcription languages.

MotionVFX in Final Cut Pro - Image Credit: Apple

Motion also gains its own MotionVFX plug-ins, assisting with color grading and 3D camera tracking. Compressor adds the option to encode Cinematic mode video recorded on an iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo.

As well as working on images from Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro adds Generate Fill, which can edit images based on a user's description. Those generated elements can be inserted as new layers, or merged into existing ones, complete with intelligent masking.

Logic Pro improvements

Logic Pro benefits from a new design that uses Liquid Glass, complete with translucent surfaces.

When it comes to actual features, Logic Pro for Mac gains a new assistant powered by Apple's models as well as those of OpenAI. The assistant can help users navigate workflows, create new songs, set up vocal tracks, or update existing projects.

There's also a redesigned browser that centralizes loops, instruments, and effect patches. An on-device audio analysis tool called "music understanding" can also automatically analyze, classify, and tag sounds added to a user's collection.

The new assistant and design of Logic Pro - Image Credit: Apple

Stem Splitter is being updated with the ability to isolate, replace, or rebalance drum parts, without needing the original multitracks.

A Producer Pack can also be unlocked from the King of Modern Salsa, Sergio George. In the pack, George discusses his signature piano sound, as well as Latin jazz and salsa loops.

Lastly, Voice Memo Sound Studio can reduce room ambience and background noise in recordings from supported iPhone models. Those clips can then be further fine-tuned in Logic Pro.

More AI, more formats

Continuing the AI push, the intelligent assistant based on Apple and OpenAI models is also available in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant can understand document contexts.

In Keynote, it can help design, animate, and refine slides, while in Pages it can draft, restructure, and fine-tune written content. Under Numbers, it can recommend suitable charts and create custom tables using world knowledge.

There's also MCP support, allowing external AI agents and tools to read content, make edits, and perform automations in the iWork package.

Beyond AI, the Content Hub also includes Apple-curated stock video footage, more templates, and themes. Keynote gains support for the Keynote Interchange Format (.keyx), and Freeform adds text styles for one-step formatting.

The updates to Apple Creator Studio will be arriving in November, free for existing subscribers.

Apple Creator Studio costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year, with education customers paying $2.99 per month or $29.99 per year.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro sales beat iPhone 17 Pro figures, but only because of China
items.content_html:
Contrary to complaints from stock analysts about poor iPhone 18 Pro sales, new supply chain research claims that the demand for the iPhone 18 Pro has been high in China, making up for some weakness elsewhere.

It was already clear that the iPhone 18 Pro had sold well as it appears to have been key to Apple reaching a $5 trillion market valuation. But in a note sent to AppleInsider, Counterpoint Research says that demand has been more patchy and region-specific than with the iPhone 17 Pro.

Sales of the iPhone 18 Pro models in China over the first three weeks after release were up 29% year over year. That was helped, though, by how Apple had more stocks of the new model than they had of the iPhone 17 Pro at launch.

Also, demand for Android smartphones from local Chinese firms fell because of price increases.

This clearly made the iPhone more appealing in China. But the demand in that country was such that the iPhone 18 Pro's overall global sales were up 3.1% compared to the iPhone 17 Pro.

These figures are all for the initial demand of the iPhone models and Counterpoint's associate director Sujeong Lim cautions that "Whether China's outperformance reflects durable demand or front-loaded buying will become clearer in the coming weeks."

Lim also says that the research firm is looking to see whether the iPhone Duo's later launch than the other models will cannibalize sales, or generate fresh, incremental demand.

Taking China out of the equation

Counterpoint Research says that in the US, sales were down 4% year over year, and speculates that this is because buyers didn't find sufficient improvements to warrant upgrading for. However, 4% is more likely to be the number of US buyers who elected to wait for the iPhone Duo instead of buying the iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Then there was also a dramatic downturn in Japan as sales there were 27% down from the iPhone 17 Pro's figures. However, that was reportedly due in part to increased iPhone prices being exacerbated by higher exchange rates.

As ever, the iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for the majority of sales across every territory. Although for the 2026 iPhones, 56% were the Max edition, compared to 57% in 2025.

This time Apple split its launch so that it only released the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the new iPhone Duo. The usual base iPhone 18 model will now be launched sometime early in 2027.

One analyst believes this split means Apple has lost sales that it won't get back, which doesn't make sense to us, given the seasonality of the iPhone market. Others have reported that Apple has cut iPhone 18 Pro orders, although JP Morgan analysts have dismissed those claims.

A Navy SEAL helps his nephew face bullies and build confidence in "Way of the Warrior Kid."

items.title: MacBook Neo 2 now predicted to arrive before summer 2027
items.content_html:
A new report claims that Apple is planning to release a second generation of its hit MacBook Neo in the first half of 2027.

The original MacBook Neo was released in March 2026 and proved to be an enormous success. It was such a hit that there was immediately a belief that a next-generation model would follow, and even unsupported wishful thinking that it would be a touch-screen one.

Now Bloomberg is reporting that the second generation MacBook Neo will launch in the first half of 2027. There are no further details in this report, nor any more precise schedule.

Previously, however, Bloomberg has claimed that the MacBook Neo 2 would be based on an A19 processor and feature 12GB of RAM. The current model uses a A18 Pro processor with 8GB RAM.

Reportedly, the MacBook Neo 2 will also sport a new range of colors. At present, the device is available in Blush, Citrus, Indigo, and Silver.

It can only be speculation, but it wouldn't be surprising if Apple launched the MacBook Neo 2 on the anniversary of the first one in March 2027. Then if there are no further price hikes, the MacBook Neo 2 would probably be priced the same as the current model.

When that was first launched, it cost $599 or $699, mostly depending on storage.. In June 2026, though, Apple raised both tiers by $100, citing the global chip shortage.

items.title: New iMac keeps old design but adds M6 processor
items.content_html:
Apple has launched an updated iMac for the first time since 2024, bringing this longstanding favorite up to the speeds of the latest Mac mini.

If it ain't broke, eventually update it. Apple has released its first update to the all-in-one iMac since the 2024 edition gained an M4 processor.

"iMac is the world's best all-in-one, and today it raises the bar yet again," said Shelly Goldberg, Apple's vice president of Hardware Engineering in a statement. "With the blazing performance and AI capabilities of M6 supercharging every workflow and the next generation of Apple Intelligence with Siri AI — combined with its stunning 24-inch Retina display, its gorgeous design in seven vibrant colors, and macOS 27 — the new iMac has everything users need to run their businesses, manage their lives, and bring their ideas to life."

Announced ahead of the "Pro and Tell" event that's due to feature the revised MacBook Pro, this iMac release is the next to get a new generation of Apple Silicon. As previously expected, there's been no major redesign to the chassis, which remains as it has been since 2020.

That chassis comes in the same seven colors as the previous edition:

  • Blue
  • Green
  • Pink
  • Yellow
  • Purple
  • Orange
  • Silver

There have been a series of upgrades to the iMac's connectivity, though. It now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, plus Apple says its storage is up to twice as fast as the previous model.

The new iMac with M6 comes in two main configurations:

  • 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, Dual 16-core Neural Engine, two Thunderbolt ports, from $1,499
  • 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, Dual 16-core Neural Engine, four Thunderbolt ports, 2.5 gigabit Ethernet, from $1,699

In the former, the 10-core CPU has two super cores, three performance cores, and five efficiency ones. The latter 12-core CPU has two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency ones.

Both versions start with 16GB RAM and 256GB storage. The base 10-core version can be upgraded to 24GB RAM, while the 12-core edition can go to 24GB or 32GB RAM.

That base model can be upgraded to 512GB storage or 1TB. The 12-core version can also go to 2TB storage.

By default, the 10-core edition does not come with Ethernet at all, but it can be configured with 2.5 gigabit Ethernet for $30. The 12-core version has 2.5 gigabit Ethernet as standard.

To upgrade or not

So an outside observer wouldn't notice any difference, but a user would. The jump from M4 to M6 is not as great as when the iMac went from Intel to Apple Silicon, but it is still noticeable.

It's arguable whether it's noticeable enough to be worth upgrading from the M4 edition. But that will become clearer once this iMac can be tested.

Users of the 2023 M3 edition will of course see more of an improvement. But this iMac is really aimed primarily at the remaining Intel Mac users, plus perhaps those on the original M1 Apple Silicon.

Apple says that typical uses such as photo editing are twice as fast as before, though. Overall AI computing speed has doubled, too, because of the dual 16-core Neural Engine, plus higher memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s.

Specifically for AI prompt processing in LM Studio, Apple says that the M6 iMac is five times faster than the previous M4 model. It's up to 12 times faster than the M1 iMac.

The new M6 iMac starts at $1,499. Pre-orders open on October 28, 2026, and it will ship on November 6.

items.title: ChatGPT can now manage your iCloud Calendar and iCloud emails
items.content_html:
Thanks to dedicated iCloud plugins, OpenAI's ChatGPT can now use details from your iCloud email inbox to schedule and update events in the Calendar app.

On Tuesday, following the debut of an upgraded M6 iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro, OpenAI revealed that ChatGPT has gained two new iCloud plugins. As a result, OpenAI has greatly improved ChatGPT's compatibility with iCloud email and the Apple Calendar app.

In short, ChatGPT can now read and check your iCloud inbox, create and manage emails, and more. What's even more impressive is that ChatGPT will be capable of updating events on your iCloud calendar, based on the details it can gather from your iCloud emails.

For iPhone, iPad, and Mac users, this will deliver a more personalized experience with OpenAI's virtual assistant. These new iCloud plugins also make ChatGPT more useful on Apple platforms, even beating previous attempts at integrating iOS and ChatGPT.

Well before the arrival of Siri AI, the iOS 18.2 update introduced support for a so-called ChatGPT extension. This let Siri hand off more advanced queries to ChatGPT, with explicit user approval, of course.

This partnership between Apple and OpenAI eventually became the subject of a lawsuit, during which OpenAI later revealed the ChatGPT extension had been "persistently underperforming." It's ultimately no surprise that OpenAI took the exact opposite route, instead giving its chatbot iCloud plugins.

In an X post, OpenAI says its new iCloud Mail and iCloud Calendar plugins for ChatGPT are "available on all ChatGPT plans," implying they won't be available to users without a subscription. This fact alone already puts ChatGPT at a disadvantage, relative to Siri AI on iOS.

Apple's new-and-improved Siri AI, which debuted with iOS 27, already offers system-wide integration. In essence, the virtual assistant already available on newer iPhones by default can manage your iCloud emails and Calendar events without a fee.

Siri AI also supports integration with other built-in iOS and iCloud-compatible apps, including Notes, Contacts, Calendar, and more. While OpenAI's new iCloud plugins are undoubtedly a step in the right direction, ChatGPT will always fall short of what Siri AI can do on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

Apple's last update to the 24-inch iMac was in 2024, when it shifted from the original M1 to the M4 chip. Two years later, Apple has now bumped the chip up yet again, this time to the M6.

However, as usual for a spec-bump update, a lot of the iMac has remained the same instead of changing with the times. While OLED is a future prospect, it's an update to the line that's far from launch.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

As it stands, consumers now have a new model of all-in-one Mac desktop to consider purchasing.

What follows is what new elements Apple has brought to the M6 24-inch iMac, and how it fares compared to the M4 model it is replacing.
