M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Design, weight, size

The M4 24-inch iMac retained the same design as the M1 that preceded it. A second-generation device, it had the same dimensions at 18.1 inches tall and 21.5 inches wide, and 5.8 inches deep at the base.

This trend of not breaking what isn't broken continues for the M6 model, with the same style and dimensions.

For weight, the -core M4 model was 9.79 pounds, and the 8-core was lighter at 9.74 pounds. The M6 model is practically the same at 9.7 pounds for the 10-core version and 9.8 pounds for the 12-core version.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: The design remains unchanged. - Image Credit: Apple

That said, we are talking about a computer that sits on a desk and won't move. Weight doesn't really matter that much.

The design is, too, unchanged between the generations. There's a thin bezel and a chunky chin on all models, with a camera hole at the top of the display.

To the rear, the M4 model had two or four visible USB Type-C connections, depending on the configuration, and a headphone jack. Once again, this is unchanged for the M6.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Display

Much like the physical design, there's no real change for the display either. Both versions have a 23.5-inch 4.5K Retina display, with a resolution of 4,480 by 2,520 pixels and a pixel density of 218 pixels per inch.

Brightness is also unchanged at 500 nits, with there also being Wide Color (P3) support and True Tone too.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: The M6 iMac color range - Image Credit: Apple

The M4 model's four-port variant did introduce a Nano-texture glass option, referring to the etching feature to minimize glare and reflections.

Naturally, the M6 model has this too, again reserved for the four-port version.

It's doubtful that any spec bump update of the iMac will include a new display unless there's a major redesign, a new size option, or OLED eventually makes its way to the model.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Performance

The real change for this model is the chip, with the move from M4 to M6.

The M4 model was sold in two varieties. One was M4 with the 8-core CPU, with four performance and four efficiency cores, as well as the 8-core GPU.

The other was a 10-core CPU with four performance cores and six efficiency cores, and a 10-core GPU. Both versions also have a Media Engine, 16-core Neural Engine, and 120GB/s of memory bandwidth.

The M6 is also available in two variants.

M4 iMac

The M4 iMac has a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display and comes in seven colors.
Buy at Amazon
Buy at B&H
Buy at Expercom

The lower-tier version of the M6 has a ten-core CPU with two super cores, three performance cores, and five efficiency cores. The upper-tier version brings the total to 12, with two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores.

There is also a difference with the GPU, as the 10-core version has a ten-core GPU while the 12-core has a 12-core GPU. The M6 also benefits from Neural Accelerators in each GPU core, which significantly improves AI workloads.

The memory on the M4 starts at 16GB, with 24GB available as a maximum for the 8-core model and 32GB for the 10-core version. This doesn't change for the M6, with the same options available.

Geekbench single-core results

While we don't have benchmarks from the M6 iMac to work with immediately, we can use the M6 Mac mini as a proxy, due to using the same M6 chips, at least for the 12-core version.

In single-core performance, the M4 iMac scores 3,175 in its eight-core CPU variant, and 3,245 in the ten-core version. The M6 Mac mini scores 4,002.

Geekbench multi-core results

For multi-core, the iMac achieves 13,405 for the eight-core variant, 15,424 in its ten-core. The M6 Mac mini again pulls ahead with 21,881.

On GPU performance using Metal, the M4 iMac gets to 47,302 and 52,961, for the eight-core and ten-core GPU, respectively. On M6, its 89,375.

Geekbench Metal results

Overall, that's a bit of a jump up in terms of processing performance, and users will certainly welcome it.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Camera and audio

On the M4, the 12MP Center Stage camera is used for FaceTime. Capable of 1080p video, it also benefits from the advanced image signal processor for a better overall image.

Apple hasn't changed this for the M6 model, as you get exactly the same camera and capabilities.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Ports around the back. - Image Credit: Apple

Audio on both models stems from a high-fidelity six-speaker system, complete with force-cancelling woofers. There's wide stereo sound and support for Spatial Audio when playing Dolby Atmos content.

To capture audio, there's the usual "studio-quality" three-mic array in place. Complete with a high signal-to-noise ratio and directional beamforming.

Apple did introduce high-impedance headphone support with the headphone jack in the M4 model, which the M6 version retains.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Storage, connectivity, peripherals

The M4 iMac offered a 256GB starting capacity, which goes up to 1TB for the 8-core model. The four-port version started at 256GB and goes up to 2TB.

This remains unchanged on the M6 model.

Depending on the chip tier you chose, there was a difference in how many things you could connect up. The lower-tier chip included two Thunderbolt 4 ports, while the upper had four of them.

The versions also differed by the use of Ethernet. The 8-core M4 model didn't have one unless you paid a $30 upgrade fee, which added it to the power brick, but this was standard for the 10-core version.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Color-matched peripherals - Image Credit: Apple

This practice continues with the M6. However, the M6 model does this with a faster 2.5Gbps Ethernet port.

On to wireless connectivity, the M4 model ships with Wi-Fi 6E, along with Bluetooth 5.3. The M6, with Apple's new N1 chip, goes up to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.

There's also a color-matched Magic Keyboard and Magic Mouse or Trackpad with each model, though here too there's a difference on the M4 depending on the chip. The keyboard has Touch ID for the 10-core model, but it's an optional extra on the 8-core model.

While we would've liked for Apple to use the Touch ID keyboard across all models, it's sticking to the existing script here.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Pricing

At launch, the M4 versions started from $1,299. However, the memory crisis meant prices had to rise in June, making the starting price $1,499 for the 8-core version, $1,699 for the 10-core

They both had 16GB of memory, 256GB of storage, and the stand instead of the VESA mount adapter.

Increasing the memory from 16GB to 24GB was $200 on both models. The 32GB was another $200 again, but it later became unavailable from Apple.

For storage, the 256GB to 512GB upgrade was $200, with 1TB a further $300. On the upper-tier M4 chip, it cost $500 to get from 1TB to 2TB.

The Magic Mouse was included by default, but you could pay an extra $50 to get the Magic Trackpad instead.

The Magic Keyboard without Touch ID could be updated to the Touch ID and Numeric Keypad edition for $80 for the 8-core model. It was $30 to upgrade the Touch ID-equipped Magic Keyboard to include the Numpad on the 10-core version.

Going from Standard glass to Nano-texture was a $200 upgrade, but only on the 10-core M4 model. Adding Ethernet to the 8-core model was $30.

The M6 versions are practically identical when it comes to the initial pricing levels of $1,299 and $1,499. They're also the same when it comes to memory upgrades, storage increases, and things like Nano-texture and keyboard changes.

Even the faster 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet option for the 10-core model is still only $30.

If you've got an Apple Silicon iMac, should you upgrade?

The last time we discussed the upgrade from the M1 iMac to the M4 iMac, the performance upgrade wasn't really enough to warrant M1 users moving to a new model.

However, the change is more significant this time from M1. The M6 is a much bigger jump, and thanks to those Neural Accelerators, it's a much better way to work with AI and machine learning tasks.

M6 24-inch iMac vs M4 24-inch iMac: Externally the same, internally different - Image Credit: Apple

The original M1 iMac was a great design at the time, and the M4 continued using it successfully. We could say the same for the M6 iMac, though the lack of changes is a tad disappointing.

OLED would've been nice. That's coming, but it's not clear when. New sizes wouldn't be that bad to have either.

As it stands, owners of the M1 iMac will probably see enough here to make the upgrade to M6. There's not as much change here for M4 iMac owners to make the leap, but they'd probably appreciate the product line continuing to get timely updates.

Where to buy Apple's M6 iMac and M4 iMac

Apple's new M6 iMac starts at $1,499 and will be available to preorder on October 28, 2026 at B&H Photo and Amazon.

The closeout M4 iMac is currently on sale from $1,455.99 at Amazon. A full rundown of the deals can be found in our M4 iMac Price Guide.

items.title: Amazon's new Alexa devices are outfitted with Matter & Thread
items.content_html:
Apple's HomeView hasn't shipped yet, but Amazon is already staking out more of the smart home with five new Alexa devices designed for everything from entertainment to sleep.

The October 28 announcement follows Apple's recent expansion into smart-home displays. Apple introduced HomeView earlier in October, bringing Siri AI, facial recognition, and Apple Home controls to a shared household screen.

Amazon's latest products address some of the same needs, but the company is spreading those capabilities across several devices. Alongside its traditional speakers and displays, Amazon is introducing products designed specifically for the nightstand and displaying family photos.

Echo Show 16

The Echo Show 16 leads the announcements with a 16-inch full HD display, built-in Fire TV, and a 13-megapixel camera with night vision. Amazon has redesigned its interface with customizable layouts for family calendars, photos, and smart-home controls.

Echo Show with stand

The display also comes with an optional Nanomatte finish that Amazon says reduces glare by more than 90%. Customers can use the Echo Show 16 for video calls, streaming entertainment, or as a central dashboard for connected-home accessories.

Echo Dot

The new Echo Dot gets a more significant upgrade than its familiar spherical design might suggest. Amazon has added a built-in smart-home hub supporting Zigbee and Matter, along with a Thread border router.

Echo Dot

The Thread border router connects compatible Matter-over-Thread accessories to the home's IP network without requiring another Thread border router for a supported Alexa setup. Previous standard Echo Dot models could control certain Matter devices but didn't provide that Thread connectivity themselves.

Amazon has also added its AZ3 processor and a fourth microphone to improve voice recognition. The company claims the speaker produces 50% more bass than its predecessor, while a built-in eero Wi-Fi extender can expand coverage for customers with an existing eero network.

Echo Studio with Home Camera

The Echo Studio with Home Camera adds visual recognition to Amazon's premium speaker. Alexa+ can identify objects placed in front of the camera, answer questions about them, and let customers check on a room remotely through the Alexa app.

Echo Studio with Home Camera

Amazon plans to add video calling through compatible Fire TV devices in a future update. The speaker has a dedicated button to disable its camera and microphones, along with an indicator light that activates when images or video are streamed to the cloud.

Echo Time

Echo Time brings Alexa+ to the bedside through a 3.2-inch circular touchscreen with customizable clock faces. Unlike Amazon's camera-equipped speakers and displays, the new clock doesn't include a camera.

Echo Time

Instead, Echo Time uses optional sleep sensing powered by Amazon's Omnisense technology. Amazon says ultrasound can detect breathing patterns and help the clock choose a wake-up time during lighter sleep, within a window of 10 to 60 minutes around a scheduled alarm.

Alexa Photo Frame

Alexa Photo Frame is a separate 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen designed to display pictures from Amazon Photos. Customers can automatically sync selected albums, while Alexa+ can find photos of particular people, pets, or events using natural-language requests.

Alexa Photo Frame

Amazon is also introducing Alexa Home Map, an interactive 3D view of a house and its connected accessories. The interface places lights, locks, cameras, and other devices in their actual locations, allowing customers to control them directly from the map.

Setting up the interior map involves scanning rooms with a compatible iPhone. Amazon plans to introduce the feature in preview later in 2026 through its iOS app and other supported devices.

How Amazon's approach compares with Apple

Amazon's new Echo Show 16 enters a market where Apple is preparing to sell its first dedicated smart-home display. AppleInsider has already compared HomeView with Amazon's Echo Show 8, but the new 16-inch model offers a substantially larger screen with Fire TV built in.

HomeView takes a different approach with a 7-inch display and deeper integration with Apple's existing devices. Siri AI can use personal information from a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, including calendars, messages, and other app content.

Apple says HomeView displays sensitive personal information only after recognizing the user's face and detecting a nearby, recently unlocked iPhone or iPad paired to that person.

The companies also differ in how they handle visual information. Apple says HomeView processes facial and voice recognition inside protected hardware on its A18 chip, while Amazon's Echo Studio uses cloud processing for visual features and provides controls to disable its camera.

Both companies are making conversational AI central to their home products, although some capabilities depend on subscriptions or software updates. Certain Amazon features require Alexa+, which is included with Prime, while Siri AI is available in beta on HomeView and won't reach HomePod mini 2 until a future update.

Pricing and availability

Amazon announced the five devices on October 28, 2026. Four are available now, while the Echo Show 16 is open for preorder.

The Echo Dot costs $99.99, while the Amazon Kids version starts at $109.99. The Echo Studio with Home Camera is available for $249.99, and the standard Echo Studio without a camera remains available for $219.99.

The Echo Time is available for $199.99, with an Amazon Kids version starting at $209.99. The Alexa Photo Frame starts at $199.99 for the black model, while Birch and Walnut wood-frame options cost $229.

The Echo Show 16 starts at $499.99, or $569.99 with the Nanomatte display. Amazon is offering $100 off preorders, with shipping expected later in 2026.

Apple's competing HomeView starts at $299 and is scheduled to ship November 13, 2026. The HomePod mini 2 costs $149 and begins shipping October 30.

items.title: Don't wait to update: iOS 27.2 brings security fixes over 130 vulnerabilities
items.content_html:
Apple's iOS 27.2 update protects your data and stops malicious apps from accessing your camera and Bluetooth without permission. Here's why you should update.

On Monday, only days after the iPhone Duo reached customers, Apple made iOS 27.2 available for download. The update includes well over 130 security enhancements, and 25 of them prevent attackers from accessing sensitive user data.

Notably, Apple patched an Accounts and App Intents issue that made it possible for apps to view private user information. The two vulnerabilities were resolved with additional entitlement checks, says Apple's website.

Authorization issues with the App Store, CloudKit, Photos storage, Quick Look, Shortcuts, and Siri were addressed through improved state management. Apple also resolved a privacy vulnerability in the Contacts app by removing sensitive data and fixed permissions issues with the Calendar and CoreMedia frameworks.

Similar now-patched vulnerabilities were found in the FileProvider, Files, FontParser, HomeKit, MediaAnalysis, ReplayKit, and Safety Check frameworks. None of the aforementioned issues were actively exploited by attackers, and all of them are resolved as of the release of iOS 27.2.

Additionally, Apple resolved a Hide My Email vulnerability that left the user's original email address exposed, even while using the feature. Improved restrictions were put in place to address the logic issue, says the company.

Meanwhile, a now-resolved Maps security issue made it possible for select apps to see all the applications installed on an iPhone. iOS 27.2 fixes this vulnerability by moving this data to a private location.

Monday's software update also stops attackers from accessing users' Photos libraries, thanks to additional entitlement checks. The System Settings app, meanwhile, received an update that prevents malicious apps from accessing restricted system interfaces.

Similarly, Apple included four security patches that stop applications from bypassing users' Privacy preferences. The now-resolved issues were present in the Accounts and Photos Storage frameworks, the kernel, and Spotlight.

iOS 27.2 stops apps from accessing Bluetooth and using the camera

While many of the fixes present in the iOS 27.2 update involve keeping user data safe, some of the security enhancements prevent bad actors from accessing key hardware features.

For instance, enhanced access restrictions in iOS 27.2 prevent maliciously crafted applications from accessing the iPhone's cameras without user knowledge or permission.

Similarly, Apple patched an AccessorySetupKit framework issue that let malicious apps access Bluetooth without explicit user permission. This authentication vulnerability was addressed through improvements to state management.

Apple's iOS 27.2 prevents denial-of-service attacks, arbitrary code execution, more

Another now-patched Bluetooth vulnerability made it possible for attackers in physical proximity to cause denial-of-service attacks. Improved validation was used for the null pointer dereference.

In total, the iOS 27.2 update includes six patches that prevent denial-of-service (DOS) attacks, affecting the Mail app, SceneKit, and Wi-Fi framework.

Monday's iOS update also includes multiple enhancements to prevent arbitrary code execution, memory corruption, unexpected app and system terminations, Web sandbox escapes, and more. The full list of security fixes is available on Apple's website.

Overall, iOS 27.2 includes well over 130 fixes, targeting a wide variety of vulnerabilities. Unlike other iOS releases, though, Monday's software update doesn't include fixes for vulnerabilities that were used in targeted attacks.

Even so, AppleInsider recommends installing the iOS 27.2 update to ensure your devices have the latest security enhancements.

items.title: It was the right time to add touch to the MacBook Pro, says John Ternus
items.content_html:
Apple has long resisted bringing touch support to the Mac, but it's finally made the jump with the new MacBook Pro. It's all because Apple felt it was the right time to make the change.

The MacBook line has been one of the most desired products to gain touch support for years. After countless rumors about it, Apple added the functionality to the PROLED versions.

However, making the change wasn't something that was done on a whim. According to a report from Wired, it needed the metaphorical planets to align first.

"The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard," insists CEO John Ternus, commenting on the years of insistence by Apple that it wasn't going to make a touch-enabled MacBook.

Even so, Ternus admits "I think there's times when it's comfortable and handy to have touch" on a notebook.

When it comes to actually making the change, Ternus claims Apple needed to "get to a point where adding touch didn't make the product lesser in any way." Apple didn't want a heavier or thicker device as a trade-off for touch support.

"That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we've ever put into a Mac," he continued. "All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well."

This is the first-ever touch-screen Mac - image credit: Apple.

To Greg Joswiak, touch was an overdue feature for some of its users, especially those in creative and engineering careers. They really wanted to work with the screen more directly.

"Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone," Joswiak said, meaning they're already naturally used to touch. "There's a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch."

Fixing wobble

Johny Srouji, chief of hardware, believes the quality of Apple's touchscreen is exceptional versus the rest of the market, because it does the hard work.

"If you're working on something easy, you're wasting your time," said Srouji. He wants the easy work outsourced, but for Apple to keep working on the harder tasks, like the display, touch support, and custom silicon.

That ethos has resulted in changes like a new thermal system to reduce the temperature of the display ready for a user's fingertips.

Srouji is also in the belief that the typical touchscreen notebook has a "wobble" when fingers touch the screen. A new hinge system was made to keep the display stable when it's touched by users.

When it comes to whether Apple is making a statement with its fall launch roster, the hardware lead insists it's business as usual for Apple. The company is still building the best products, and will ship them when it believes it's ready and complete.

items.title: Apple acknowledges social media reports of iPhone Duo screen cracking
items.content_html:
In a very brief statement, Apple says that a small number of iPhone Duo units have an issue impacting the inner display. It does not appear to be that many units impacted.

Over the weekend, there have been accounts on social media discussing iPhone Duo screen failures. They are all remarkably similar, and appear to be because of a hinge failure.

On Monday afternoon, Apple issued a brief statement about the matter.

"We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," Apple said. "If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."

In follow-up remarks, posted by Mark Gurman on X, Apple says that most units will not have the issue. Furthermore, the screen-break will happen very shortly after first opening the device.

It's not clear how many units are impacted. It's not a giant amount, though.

Since Saturday morning, we've been talking to US Apple Store Genius Bars that we've been working with for 15 years or more. While we first started with seven stores, and one infant failure as of Monday morning, this number in both regards has grown.

We have now spoken to staffers in 20 Genius Bars that we trust. That number has grown to four impacted iPhone Duo units, all with screen issues. This figure does not help you if yours is one, though.

Unfortunately, at this time, we have no visibility internationally, no data outside those 20 stores, and have no hooks inside Apple's online AppleCare apparatus.

And on Saturday we gave you the same advice, that Apple did today. If you've got an issue, you should, in fact, contact AppleCare.

So far, the four cases that we are aware of were fixed by giving the purchaser a replacement phone from service stock, which is separate from sale stock. None of the four have returned.

items.title: On OLED MacBook Pro-eve, I have just one question
items.content_html:
Apple is expected to announce its touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro on October 27. On October 26, I still find it impossible to really grasp who this machine is for and if anyone is really crying out for what seems to be a MacBook More-Pro.

There have long been rumors of Apple's plans to release a new laptop that will sit above the current 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros in its lineup. It may or may not be called the MacBook Ultra, although it seems unlikely at this point.

The name is just one question mark that continues to loom large over what should otherwise be an exciting new laptop. There's talk of an OLED display, a first for Apple's Mac lineup, as well as Apple's almost range-topping M5 Pro and M5 Max silicon.

We've also heard claims of a (slightly) new industrial design, with Apple ditching the familiar notch and replacing it with an iPhone-like Dynamic Island. A lighter, possibly even thinner construction has also been rumored.

And then, there's the main point that this laptop rumor has hung its hat on for what feels like forever. The new not-MacBook-Ultra-but-also-maybe is expected to be the first Mac with a touchscreen.

But as the 2007 meme also ponders, "y tho?"

A break from tradition

Apple, famously, once argued that touchscreen laptops were a big no-no. None other than Craig Federighi, Apple's head of software engineering, argued as much at a time when every other company was falling over themselves to bring touch to their computers.

"We really feel that the ergonomics of using a Mac are that your hands are rested on a surface, and that lifting your arm up to poke a screen is a pretty fatiguing thing to do," Federighi said when discussing the possibility of bringing touch to the Mac in June 2018. "I don't think we've looked at any of the other guys to date and said, how fast can we get there?"

He went further, arguing that Windows touchscreen laptops were nothing more than "experiments." But just two years later, things were changing.

The OLED MacBook Pro may be the end of the notch

A patent published in 2020 highlighted Apple's work to bring touch to the Mac. At the time, it was suggested that users could touch their laptop display to interact with an iPhone or similar device.

Fast-forward to October 2026, and it seems Apple is finally ready to launch a touchscreen MacBook Pro.

But again, I'm left wondering why.

More importantly, I'm wondering who such a feature is really for, and how it will actually work. Apple's macOS is designed with cursor input in mind, with small targets like window controls that just aren't built to be tapped with meaty fingers.

Apple already makes software that's built with a touch-first mindset. It's called iPadOS, and you can get it right now on an array of computers called iPads.

You can even try it out a bit with Sidecar. It's pretty nasty business, though, unless you're using an Apple Pencil.

I'd argue that Apple was right the first time out when it said that poking a laptop display doesn't sound like a fun way to use a desktop or laptop computer. I've yet to see a use case that makes the hassle, or the fingerprints, worth it.

There's little else here

The problem is, without the touch element, this impending MacBook Pro announcement makes even less sense. If it's going to use the same chips as the current model, and we agree that touching it is lunacy, there's little else going for it.

The move to an OLED display will be the headline-grabber, sure. OLED promises deep contrast and vibrant colors plus lightning-fast response times.

But anyone who has used one of Apple's mini-LED laptops will tell you that they already boast stunning displays. Almost too bright in some instances, with gorgeous colors and strong contrast figures.

Nobody accused Apple's Liquid Display XDR of lacking brightness or anything else

If the move to OLED brings the end of the notch, then so be it. But I don't foresee many MacBook Pro buyers ditching their current laptop just to get a Dynamic Island.

And if the new model does use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, it won't be any faster than its predecessor, either. Yet it'll presumably command a higher price.

Which again raises the question, "y tho?" I could get behind the idea of an OLED MacBook Pro if it were replacing the current models wholesale, but it doesn't appear to be the case. Apple announced a new non-OLED 14-inch MacBook Pro this very day, after all.

The way I see it, there are only two ways that the fabled OLED MacBook Pro makes sense. Either it has some knockout feature that hasn't leaked yet, or Apple has an especially compelling story for the features that have.

In lieu of either, for now at least, I'm left wondering just what market a new OLED MacBook Pro really serves.

items.title: New iPad mini shrinks just enough to complicate case compatibility
items.content_html:
Apple's new iPad mini has slimmed down with a thinner, narrower design, but those minor changes could make your perfectly good old case a lousy fit.

The OLED upgrade increases the display size from 8.3 inches to 8.5 inches while keeping roughly the same footprint. However, Apple's published measurements reveal several physical differences that could affect case compatibility.

The sixth-generation iPad mini from 2021 and the A17 Pro model from 2024 have identical dimensions of 195.4 mm tall, 134.8 mm wide, and 6.3 mm thick.

The 2026 model measures 195.3 mm tall, 132.6 mm wide, and 5.4 mm thick, according to Apple's technical specifications. The height difference is just 0.1 mm, but the reductions in width and thickness could affect how older cases grip the device.

Will older iPad mini cases still fit?

Rigid snap-on cases are the biggest concern because they rely on a close fit around the tablet's edges. A case molded for the older dimensions could leave the new iPad mini loose around the sides, although the actual fit hasn't been tested.

SpecificationiPad mini 6/7iPad mini (A20 Pro)Difference
Height195.4 mm195.3 mm0.1 mm
Width134.8 mm132.6 mm2.2 mm
Thickness6.3 mm5.4 mm0.9 mm
Display8.3 inches8.5 inches+0.2 inches

Flexible silicone and TPU cases might accommodate the smaller enclosure, but their ability to hold it securely will depend on the design. Magnetic folios are another possibility because they attach without gripping the tablet's edges.

However, it's unclear whether the magnets in older folios will align correctly with the new model. Apple's existing Smart Folio officially supports the sixth-generation and A17 Pro iPad mini models. The new A20 Pro model isn't included in that compatibility list as of 10:00 AM ET on October 26.

The company has also introduced a redesigned TechWoven Smart Folio for the 2026 iPad mini, priced at $79. It features a two-panel construction and additional viewing angles, although the new accessory doesn't establish that older magnetic covers are incompatible.

The new iPad mini becomes available November 6 starting at $699, following preorders beginning October 28. Until case manufacturers confirm compatibility with the 2026 model, buyers shouldn't assume existing cases will provide a secure fit.

items.title: macOS 27.2 is out with cosmetic changes, new Siri AI languages
items.content_html:
After weeks of testing, Apple has released macOS Golden Gate 27.2. Officially it's a minor release, but under the hood changes are preparing the way for touch-screen Macs.

As previously revealed during the beta testing period, macOS 27.2 has introduced a cosmetic change to Apple Music. It's part of a wider rebrand that includes a new video sting for music productions. Now that macOS 27.2 has been released as the official current OS for the Mac, there are a few visual changes.

Apple Music's logo and refreshed color scheme is the most visible update, with the old red highlights being replaced by blue. But there are also changes to the volume and brightness controls.

If you access those through the keyboard, they now step down in small but distinct steps instead of on a continuous line.

More significantly, Siri AI has been updated to support five more languages:

  • French
  • Japanese
  • Korean
  • Portuguese
  • Spanish

There are also general performance security updates, plus bug fixes.

What will ultimately make this a notable release, though, is that it includes many features to do with touch control. This is the release that features touch tools inside Apple apps such as Safari and Photos.

They're not apparent yet, as in Apple does not describe or demonstrate them. But they mean that macOS Golden Gate is now ready for the expected OLED touch-screen version of MacBook Pro.

The new macOS 27.2 runs on the same list of Macs that support version 27. It's the macOS edition that will now come pre-installed on all new Macs.

If your Mac is able to run macOS 27.2, you will be prompted to update to it. However, it can be weeks before you're prompted, and you can instead go to System Settings, General, Software Update to request it be installed now.

However, AppleInsider always recommends that you wait at least a few days after a macOS update. Even a comparatively minor one is significant because the OS touches everything and any problems can be severe.

Wait for other users to find those problems, and for Apple to fix them.

items.title: iOS 27.2 is out without the Apple Health revamp
items.content_html:
Apple's first major update to iOS 27 has arrived, with iOS 27.2 bringing FaceTime Dual Capture and an Apple Music logo change, but no Apple Health revamp.

Following four developer beta cycles and one release candidate build, Apple is now making the update for iOS 27.2 available to the public. The update is available to all iPhones that are compatible with iOS 27 at the time of its launch.

The upgrade is unusual in that it jumps over iOS 27.1 in favor of iOS 27.2. The reality is that Apple has been using iOS 27.1 with the iPhone Duo due to its foldable dual-screen design, and has kept that model separated from the main group for launch.

With the actual release of iOS 27.2, both iPhone Duo and regular iPhones get the update:

  • The release build of iOS 27.2 is 24B119 for the standard iPhones, replacing the release candidate 24B115.
  • The release build of iOS 27.2 is 24B91020 for the iPhone Duo.

What's new in iOS 27.2

The first developer beta introduced a redesigned Health app, which would work alongside the health sensing systems of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the Apple Watch Series 12. However, by the fourth developer beta, Apple removed it entirely, intending to install it later.

The first beta also had expanded Siri AI localization, which made it able to work in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

FaceTime benefited from Dual Capture support, so that users can share video feeds from both front-facing and rear iPhone cameras on compatible models.

The Apple TV app also gained profiles, matching tvOS 26.2 but on the iPhone. Existing Apple TV profiles could be used, with the app also allowing you to create brand new ones, too.

The second developer beta also included the initial workings for an AutoLock security feature. If the iPhone detected multiple signals, such as a sudden and sharp acceleration, the inaccessibility of a paired Apple Watch, or a prolonged loss of network activity, the iPhone would automatically lock.

However, at the time of that beta, the iPhone would detect the signals in the background, but wouldn't actually lock the device. It seems this was to test that the feature detected threats and avoided false positives.

Aside from the loss of the redesigned Apple Health app, the fourth developer beta also removed all color from the Apple Music icon, making it a black note on a white background. There was also a new setting for HomePods, with a new slider to Lock Controls to prevent touch interactions with the smart home device.

How to install iOS 27.2 on an iPhone

To install iOS 27 on an iPhone, open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update. Tap the iOS 27.2 update and follow the instructions.

Users of earlier operating system versions that have yet to move over to the iOS 27 generation will be prompted to move over, if their iPhone is compatible.
